title: Student notes: anagama wood-fired kilns
bodyMd:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes.

- An anagama kiln is a single-chamber wood-fired kiln built along a slope.
- A single firing lasts several days; potters feed wood into it continuously, day and night.
- Ash thrown off by the burning wood settles on the pots and melts into a glaze.
- Ash falls unevenly inside the chamber, so no two pots from one firing come out alike.
- Ceramicist Junko Mori fires an anagama kiln twice a year in Oregon.
- Mori says the kiln, not the potter, makes the final decision about a pot's surface.
accessibilityText: A list of six research notes taken by a student about anagama kilns. One: an anagama kiln is a single-chamber wood-fired kiln built along a slope. Two: a single firing lasts several days, with potters feeding wood continuously, day and night. Three: ash thrown off by the burning wood settles on the pots and melts into a glaze. Four: ash falls unevenly inside the chamber, so no two pots from one firing come out alike. Five: ceramicist Junko Mori fires an anagama kiln twice a year in Oregon. Six: Mori says the kiln, not the potter, makes the final decision about a pot's surface.

provenance.notes: Original note set written for this item bank. The ceramicist and her quoted remark are invented; the description of wood-ash glazing is general background, not adapted from any source.
